newsitem.title: GERMANY: Early German tax deal possible -CDU's Schaeuble.
newsitem.headline: Early German tax deal possible -CDU's Schaeuble.

text.p: Early agreement on Germany's controversial proposed tax reform is still possible, a senior government figure said on Monday after opposition Social Democrats (SPD) laid out their tax proposals.

Wolfgang Schaeuble, parliamentary leader of Chancellor Helmut Kohl's Christian Democrats (CDU), told a news briefing that he saw some positive aspects in the SPD plan, which sets out a budget-neutral restructuring of the tax system.
"(There are) some starting positions for a quick agreement," Schaeuble told a news briefing called directly after the SPD's conference on its tax plans.

Talks between the SPD and the government on a planned 30 billion mark ($18 billion) tax reform broke down in April after the SPD said the package failed to attack Germany's high non-wage labour costs, seen as a cause of the country's high jobless rate.
The government is anxious for the reform to be implemented starting from next year.

But unless it can wring an agreement out of the SPD in further talks, it faces a parliamentary battle in which its rival party has control of the upper chamber, whose support the tax reform bill requires.
Earlier, the SPD set out plans to restructure some 78 billion marks of revenues in the tax system, giving tax breaks to families and workers while raising revenues elsewhere.

Around 48 billion marks of tax reductions would come through measures including a cut in the basic rate of income tax from 25.9 percent to 15 percent and a reduction in taxes on reinvesting corporate profit from 45 percent to 35 percent.

SPD chief Oskar Lafontaine however continued to insist that a reduction in the 53 percent tax bracket was only possible if it could be financed elsewhere. He added the government's plans to cut the top tax bracket to 39 percent could not be financed. ($ = 1.685 German Marks)
